lines.translation: #tr.en: “Destroy (your) house, build a boat;
#tr.en:  “Spurn property, save life!

variants.reconstruction:
%n elep (|) teppušu | e[ṣ]eršī-ma || eṣerti | k[i]ppātim
#note:  The interpretation of @i{e}[@i{ṣ}]@i{eršī-ma} as an imperative follows @bib{RN3182@299}: “Draw out the boat that you will make/ On a circular plan”. We take @i{eṣerti k}[@i{i}]@i{ppātim} as a predicative complement (on this category, see the comment on OB I 1). @bib{wasserman2020flood@69} understands @i{e}[@i{ṣ}]@i{eršī-ma} as a first person, but also takes @akk{e-[ṣ]e-er-ti ki-[i]p-pa-tim} as a predicative.

lines.translation: #tr.en: “Her base should be one @i{ikû} (ca. 3,600 m²); [her] hull (lit. walls) should be one @i{nindanu} (ca. 6 m) (high).

variants.reconstruction:
%n kannū | ašlā | ṭam[û]ša?
#note: Compare the reading of this line suggested by Finkel in his edition of the fragment (@bib{RN1780@359}): @akk{ka-an-nu aš-la-a ta-mu-u[r] ša [MA₂]}, “You saw @i{kannu} ropes and @i{ašlu} ropes/rushes for [a coracle before!].” The reading is problematic, as it would result in @i{kannu} used for the accusative, as noted by @bib{RN2399@253 fn. 6} or as @i{casus pendens}, in the interpretation of @bib{streck2017review@140} (“Ropes, each (one) @i{ašlu} long – (when) you have found (them) for [the ship(?)], then may somebody twist …”). @bib{george2016review@445} suggests reading @akk{ka-an-nu aš-la-a <lu> ṭa₂-mu-u₂# [a-na ŠA₃]-ša₂}, “[Let] tapes, each 120 cubits long, be laced [inside] it.” @bib{wasserman2020flood@71} follows this reading, though he notes that @i{ṭam}/@i{wû} is unusual when referring to the preparation of ropes, as this verb virtually always refers to wool, textiles and braids (but note @i{ušandû ana gišparrīšu iṭammi ebla}, “The bird hunter plaits strands for his snare,” in @i{Palm and Vine} 21′; @url{/corpus/L/2/12}{L II.12}). All three interpreters note that @i{ašlu} is a measure of length making 10 @i{nindanum}, ca. 60 m. @bib{streck2017review@140} explains that the distributive suffix -@i{ā} (@i{ašlā}) indicates that each and every one of the @i{kannu}-cords must reach this length.

lines.translation: #tr.en: Her plaiting are @i{cords} of one @i{ašlu} each:

variants.reconstruction:
%n liptilkum | bītī | pi[t]ilt[am]
#note: For the interpretation of this line, see @bib{george2016review@445}, who suggests reading the middle word as @akk{E₂{+bi-ti}}, i.e., @i{bītī}: “Let my household plait the palm fibre into ropes for you.” George interprets this as Ea offering his temple personnel to help Atram-ḫasīs construct the boat. See also @bib{wasserman2020flood@72}. Compare the different interpretation offered in @bib{RN1780@359}: @akk{li-ip-ti-ik-kum GIŠ ar₂#-ti pi₂-[t]i-il-tam}, “Let someone (else) twist the fronds and palm-fibre for you!”

variants.reconstruction:
%n šalāšā | ṣēlī! || ina libbīša | a[d]di
#note: @akk{ṣe-ri} has been interpreted as a writing of @i{ṣēlī}, “ribs” (so Finkel, cf. also @bib{RN2399@253 fn. 6}; @bib{streck2017review@141b} and @bib{streck2018man@11 fn. 35}). Note, however, that the parallels adduced there for a change /@i{l}/ > /@i{r}/ in Old Babylonian texts all refer to /@i{l}/ occurring at the offset of a closed syllable, and not in intervocalic position.

variants.reconstruction:
%n ša (išteat) (|) parsikat | ikbiru || ešret (|) ginindanak | mūrakšu
#note: Finkel understands the line as “one @i{parsiktu}-vessel thick,” i.e. “roughly one cubit (~fifty centimetres) thick” (@bib{RN1780@108, 168, 344–349})”, an understanding followed by @bib{wasserman2020flood@69}. Note, however, that, as in this line, the girth of logs is measured in capacity units in certain Old Babylonian contexts (see @bib{powell1984late@42–46}; @bib{rla_7_457b@491b}). Given the formula provided by the text @url{/library/YBC.8600}{YBC.8600} (@bib{neugebauer1945mathematical@57 Ec}), and that 1 @akk{PI} = 60 @akk{SILA₃}, then the circumference of each log would be √(60 × 0;0,12,30) = 0;27,23,10 @i{nindan}, i.e. ca. 27 cubits or 13,5 m, corresponding to a diameter of ca. 4,35 m.

variants.reconstruction:
%n uštarkib | samān (|) šār | iṭṭâm | i[n]a? kīrātīya
#note: The verb @akk{uš-ta-ar-ki-ib}, which appears in the present line and again in line 25, is the subject of divergent interpretations. George proposed an alternative reading, @akk{uš-ta-ar-ṭi-ib}, parsing it as a previously unattested III/3 stem of @i{raṭābum} and translating the action as “I melted successive batches of dried bitumen in my furnaces” to render it soft and workable (@bib{george2016review@445}). In his commentary on lines 21-23, Wasserman maintains the reading @i{uštarkib} (‘he loaded’); he interprets the depicted activity as Atraḫasīs loading bitumen into the furnaces in order to melt it for the subsequent caulking of the boat (@bib{wasserman2020flood@74}).

variants.reconstruction:
%n [...] ... rabîš ... | [...]-ma | šibqum? | aṣlal
#note: @bib{RN1780@364}  analyzes the end of the verse as @i{pi-qum aṣ-la-al}, "... I slept with difficulty.” So also @bib{joo2025roundark@053}. @bib{wasserman2020flood@75-76}, however, argues that the present tablet uses PI rather than PI₂, taking l. 60 as evidence for this spelling. However, PI₂ is in fact also attested in this tablet: already in l. 11 we find @i{pi₂-ti-il-tam}. In addition, Wasserman considers the translation of @i{pīqum} before @i{aṣlal} as “with difficulty” problematic because @i{pīqum} is never attested as an adverb. He therefore tentatively proposes reading ŠI BI QUM as @i{šibqum}, “plan, stratagem, plot, trick,” with BI for IB, an otherwise attested vowel mistake. Nevertheless, this interpretation remains uncertain, especially in light of the parallel in Gilg. XI 77–78: @i{[lā]m šamši rabê eleppu gamrat / […] šupšuqū-ma}, “[before] sundown the boat was finished. / [...] were very difficult,” where @i{šupšuqū} provides a possible parallel for the expression of difficulty.
